justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around the current S&P 500 level, which was trading near 488–491 at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I set the estimate at 490.5, essentially assuming minimal drift from the prevailing price with a slight upward lean based on recent momentum. At one week, I nudged the estimate to 492, incorporating a small positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run average daily return of equities annualized. At one month, the estimate of 495 reflects that same slow drift compounding over roughly 21 trading days, while acknowledging that over longer horizons the expected return contribution becomes more meaningful even if it remains modest in absolute price terms.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily using historical realized volatility of the S&P 500. At the one-day horizon, the 90% interval of 481–500 spans roughly 19 points, consistent with roughly 1–1.5% daily moves capturing most of the distribution under normal market conditions. The one-week interval widens to 474–510, reflecting that uncertainty scales with the square root of time, so roughly 2.3 times the daily standard deviation. The one-month interval of 460–530 is wider still, capturing approximately 4.5 times the daily standard deviation, consistent with historical monthly volatility in the 4–6% range for the index.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden macro shock such as an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a significant inflation surprise, or a deterioration in credit markets. Geopolitical escalation or a systemic financial event — the kinds of tail events that drove moves of 5–10% in single weeks during 2020 or 2022 — could easily breach the one-week or one-month bounds. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a dovish pivot in central bank communication, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could push prices through the upper end of the ranges.

It is also worth noting that these intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions with relatively stable volatility, which is a simplification. Equity markets exhibit volatility clustering and fat tails, meaning that if conditions shift to a high-volatility regime, the true 90% interval could be considerably wider than stated. The one-month horizon is particularly susceptible to this, since a single week of elevated volatility can dramatically widen the realized distribution of outcomes over the full month.
